module_title: Gathering Materials: Free Resources All Around You

lessons.title: Collecting Crop Residues: Maize Stalks, Rice Straw, and More
lessons.body: After harvest, your field is full of free compost material. Maize stalks, rice straw, sorghum stover, millet stalks, and groundnut haulms are all valuable. The key is to collect them before they are burned or eaten by livestock. For maize, cut stalks at ground level with a sharp panga or sickle. Chop them into 5-10 cm piecesâsmaller pieces decompose faster. A cubic meter of chopped maize stalks weighs about 150-200 kg. You need roughly 1 cubic meter of crop residues to make 0.5 cubic meters of finished compost. Rice straw is high in silica and decomposes slowly, so mix it with nitrogen-rich materials like animal manure or fresh grass. Never compost diseased plants (e.g., maize with smut) or seeds of aggressive weeds like striga. Store residues in a dry, covered pile or under a tarp to keep them from getting waterlogged. If you have livestock, you can also use crop residues as bedding, then compost the bedding. Collect after each harvest and keep a dedicated pile. In dry areas, residues break down slowly, so add water and turn the pile every two weeks. A good mix by volume: 3 parts crop residues to 1 part manure or fresh green matter. This gives the right carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. Start collecting todayâevery stalk is money in your soil.

lessons.title: Using Animal Manure: Cattle, Goats, Poultry, and Rabbits
lessons.body: Animal manure is the richest free fertilizer you can get. But not all manures are equal. Poultry manure (chicken, duck) is the strongest: it contains about 3-5% nitrogen, 2-3% phosphorus, and 1-2% potassium. Rabbit manure is also excellentâ2-3% nitrogenâand can be used fresh without burning plants. Goat and sheep manure are similar, around 2% nitrogen. Cattle manure is weaker (0.5-1% nitrogen) but adds lots of organic matter. Collect manure daily or weekly. For poultry, scoop it from under roosts; for cattle, from kraals or stalls. Mix manure with crop residues or bedding to prevent nitrogen loss. Never use fresh manure directly on vegetablesâit can burn roots and spread pathogens. Compost it first: pile manure with straw or leaves, keep it as moist as a wrung-out sponge, and turn every 3-4 days for 3-4 weeks. A hot pile (55-65Â°C) kills weed seeds and parasites. If you have rabbits, place their cages over a compost pileâurine and droppings fall straight in. For cattle, collect manure mixed with urine-soaked bedding. One cow produces about 10-15 kg of manure per day. A goat gives 1-2 kg. A chicken gives 0.1-0.2 kg. Even a small flock of 10 chickens gives you 1-2 kg of high-nitrogen manure daily. Store manure under cover to prevent rain washing away nutrients. Use it within 3 months for best results.

lessons.title: Kitchen and Market Waste: Fruit Peels, Vegetable Trimmings
lessons.body: Your kitchen and local market are goldmines for compost. Fruit peels (banana, mango, orange, pineapple), vegetable trimmings (tomato, onion, cabbage, carrot), coffee grounds, tea leaves, and eggshells are all excellent. These materials are high in nitrogen and decompose quickly. Collect them in a bucket with a lid to avoid flies and smells. At the market, ask vendors for spoiled produceâthey often throw away large quantities. A single market stall can generate 5-10 kg of waste per day. Mix kitchen waste with dry materials like sawdust, dry leaves, or shredded paper to absorb moisture and prevent odor. The ideal mix is 1 part kitchen waste to 2 parts dry material by volume. Avoid meat, fish, dairy, and oily foodsâthey attract rats and dogs and smell terrible. Also avoid citrus peels in large amounts; they can slow decomposition and repel worms. But small amounts are fine. If you have a worm bin, fruit and vegetable scraps are perfect worm food. Chop large pieces to speed up composting. In a hot climate, a pile with kitchen waste can heat up within 24 hours. Turn it every 2-3 days. If you run a restaurant or hotel, you can collect 20-50 kg per day. That is enough to make compost for a small farm. Always cover fresh waste with a layer of dry material or soil to keep flies away. Use within a week to avoid rotting and attracting pests.

lessons.title: Weeds, Grass Clippings, and Leaves: What to Use and Avoid
lessons.body: Weeds and grass clippings are free and abundant. But you must be careful. Use weeds before they set seed. If you pull weeds with seeds, do not compost them unless your pile gets hot enough (55-65Â°C) to kill seeds. Otherwise, seeds will spread when you use the compost. Safe weeds: amaranth, blackjack, purslane, and most broadleaf weeds before flowering. Avoid aggressive weeds like striga, couch grass, and nutgrassâtheir roots and seeds survive composting. Grass clippings are high in nitrogen. But do not use clippings from lawns treated with herbicides or pesticidesâthey can harm your compost and plants. Also avoid grass that has been sprayed with weed killer. Leaves are high in carbon. Dry leaves decompose slowly, so chop or shred them. Oak and eucalyptus leaves are acidic and slow to break down; use them in small amounts. Banana leaves, mango leaves, and most tropical leaves are fine. Collect leaves in sacks after they fall. A large tree can give you 50-100 kg of dry leaves per season. Mix leaves with grass clippings or manure to balance carbon and nitrogen. Never use leaves from diseased trees. Also avoid thorny branches unless you chop them finely. If you have a lawn, collect clippings after mowing. Let them dry for a day before adding to the pile to prevent matting. A good ratio: 2 parts dry leaves to 1 part fresh grass clippings. Turn the pile regularly. This mix heats up fast and gives rich compost in 4-6 weeks.

lessons.title: Sourcing Wood Ash, Charcoal Dust, and Bone Meal
lessons.body: Wood ash, charcoal dust, and bone meal are mineral-rich amendments. Wood ash from untreated wood contains potassium (5-10%) and calcium, plus trace minerals. It raises soil pH, so use it on acidic soils. Do not use ash from charcoal briquettes (they contain chemicals) or from treated or painted wood. Collect ash from your cooking fire or local bakeries. Store it dryâmoisture makes it lose potency. Add small amounts to compost: 1 cup per 10 kg of compost. Too much ash can make compost alkaline. Charcoal dust (from charcoal production or crushing charcoal) is pure carbon. It does not add nutrients but improves soil structure and holds nutrients. Mix it into compost at 5-10% by volume. It also absorbs odors. Bone meal is made from crushed, steamed animal bones. It is high in phosphorus (15-20%) and calcium. You can make it at home: boil bones to remove meat, dry them in the sun, then crush with a hammer or grind. It is slow-release, so add it to compost or directly to planting holes. A handful per plant is enough. If you cannot make bone meal, ask butcheries for bones. Wood ash and bone meal are especially good for root crops like carrots, onions, and potatoes. Store all three in dry containers. Use ash within 6 months; bone meal lasts a year if kept dry. These materials turn waste into valuable fertilizer.

lessons.title: Making a Materials Collection Plan for Your Business
lessons.body: To run a compost business, you need a steady supply of materials. Start by mapping your sources. Walk around your neighborhood, market, farms, and livestock keepers. Make a list: who has crop residues? Who has manure? Who has kitchen waste? Talk to them. Offer to collect for free or pay a small fee. For example, a market vendor might pay to have waste removed; you can charge a small collection fee and get free material. A cattle keeper might give you manure if you clean the kraal. Set a weekly schedule. For a small business producing 1 ton of compost per month, you need about 3 tons of raw materials. That is roughly: 1.5 tons crop residues, 0.5 tons manure, 0.5 tons kitchen waste, 0.5 tons leaves/grass. Use a notebook to record collection dates, quantities, and sources. Invest in tools: a wheelbarrow, sacks, a rake, a fork, and a tarpaulin. Keep a dedicated collection area with separate piles for carbon-rich (dry) and nitrogen-rich (wet) materials. Build your compost pile in layers: 15 cm dry, 10 cm wet, sprinkle ash or bone meal, repeat. Water and turn. Train a helper if needed. Also, consider making arrangements with restaurants, schools, and hotels for regular pickup. A signed agreement ensures steady supply. Track your costs: transport, labor, sacks. Even if materials are free, collection costs money. Price your compost to cover costs and give profit. A 50 kg bag of good compost can sell for $10-20 in many African cities. With a good plan, you turn waste into wealth.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Gathering Materials for Organic Fertilizer & Compost in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into one working document you can print, pin in your store, and use when training staff or buying agents. The focus is deliberately business-first: every material decision should reduce your input cost per tonne, protect your compost quality, and keep you compliant with buyers who increasingly ask where your feedstock comes from. Across sub-Saharan Africa, the same materials are everywhere â the difference between a profitable compost enterprise and a struggling one is usually not access, but organisation: knowing what to collect, where, when, at what cost, and in what quantity.

Use the two reference tables below to price and prioritise your feedstock, then work through the checklist and the collection plan to convert scattered free resources into a reliable supply chain.

1. Feedstock Value and Sourcing at a Glance

Table 1: Common compost feedstocks in Africa â carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, moisture, and sourcing notes
Material Approx. C:N ratio Moisture Sourcing reality in Africa
Maize stalks & cobs 60:1 (stalks), 40:1 (cobs) Low (10â20%) Abundant after harvest; often burned in field. Bale or chop within 2 weeks to avoid termite and mould loss.
Rice straw 70:1 Low (10â15%) Large volumes in irrigated schemes (e.g. Mwea, Kilombero, Office du Niger). High silica slows decomposition â chop to 5â10 cm.
Cattle manure (fresh) 15:1 High (70â80%) Zero-grazing and dairy zero-grazing units give the most consistent supply. Watch for veterinary drug residues.
Goat & sheep manure 12:1 Medium (50â60%) Often mixed with bedding; excellent nutrient density. Collect from kraals weekly to preserve nitrogen.
Poultry litter 8:1 Medium (30â40%) Very high nitrogen and salt. Use as an activator at 10â20% of pile volume only.
Rabbit manure 12:1 Medium (30â40%) Can be applied fresh without burning plants; ideal for premium vermicompost lines.
Fruit & vegetable waste 20:1 Very high (80â90%) Market dumps and juice bars. Collect daily; high leachate risk and smell if left uncomposted.
Grass clippings & leaves 20â40:1 Medium Lawns, roadsides, agroforestry prunings. Avoid diseased or herbicide-treated material.
Wood ash N/A (mineral) Dry From kitchens, bakeries, brick kilns. Raises pH; limit to 2â5% of pile volume.
Charcoal dust N/A (mineral) Dry From charcoal depots and markets. Improves aeration and water retention; not a nutrient source.
Bone meal ~3:1 (N:P) Dry Butcheries and abattoirs. Must be boiled, dried, and ground â see safety warning below.

Sources: FAO, "On-farm composting methods" (2003); Cornell University Waste Management Institute, "Composting: Fundamentals and Applications"; KALRO (Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation) technical bulletins on manure management; NARS/AGRA soil health training materials.

2. Collection Logistics and Cost Model

The second table translates agronomy into business arithmetic. Fill in your own figures â the per-tonne delivered cost is the number that decides whether a material is genuinely "free".

Table 2: Indicative collection logistics and delivered cost model per tonne (2024 estimates, East/West Africa)
Material Typical distance Transport mode Labour (person-days/t) Indicative delivered cost (USD/t)
Maize stalks (baled) 5â15 km Pickup / tractor trailer 1.5 8â15
Rice straw (loose) 10â30 km Lorry 2.0 12â20
Cattle manure 2â10 km Wheelbarrow / pickup 1.0 5â12
Poultry litter 5â20 km Pickup 1.0 6â14
Market vegetable waste 1â5 km Handcart / tricycle 0.8 3â8
Grass clippings 0â5 km Handcart 0.5 2â6
Wood ash 0â10 km Sacks / pickup 0.4 2â5
Bone meal (processed) 5â20 km Pickup 3.0 (incl. processing) 25â45

Sources: Author's synthesis from AGRA "Africa Agriculture Status Report" (2022) input cost data; FAO "Composting for smallholder farmers" field guides; interviews with compost enterprises in Kenya, Ghana, and Uganda (2023â2024). Figures are indicative and vary with fuel prices and season.

3. What to Use and What to Avoid

Use freely: cereal stalks and cobs, rice straw, legume haulms, cattle/goat/rabbit manure, poultry litter (in moderation), market and kitchen vegetable waste, grass clippings, tree leaves (except those listed below), wood ash, charcoal dust, and properly processed bone meal.

Avoid or pre-treat: meat, dairy, and oily kitchen waste (attracts rodents and flies); diseased plant material; herbicide-treated grass (residues can persist for months); glossy or coloured paper; plastic, glass, and metal; human sewage unless fully treated and permitted; and manure from animals recently treated with persistent veterinary antibiotics.

Handle with care: eucalyptus, neem, and some acacia leaves contain allelopathic compounds that slow decomposition â compost them separately or use in small proportions. Pine needles are extremely acidic and slow to break down.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Bone Meal and Manure Handling

Raw bone meal and fresh manure can carry anthrax spores, Salmonella, E. coli, and Brucella. In regions with known anthrax outbreaks (parts of East and Southern Africa), never handle raw bones or carcass material without official veterinary clearance. Boil bones for at least 30 minutes, dry them fully in the sun, and grind only while wearing a P2/N95 respirator, gloves, and eye protection. Always wear gloves and closed shoes when turning manure or compost, and wash hands and tools with soap after every session. Keep children and livestock away from the compost pad.

4. Making a Materials Collection Plan for Your Business

A collection plan converts "free" materials into a forecastable input. Work through these five steps each season:

  1. Map your sources within a 20 km radius. List every farm, market, abattoir, poultry house, and mill. Note what they produce, how much, and when.
  2. Estimate volumes and timing. Maize stalks arrive in one burst after harvest; market waste arrives daily. Match your collection schedule to both.
  3. Negotiate access early. A simple written agreement â even a signed note â prevents a competitor from taking your straw after you have invested in baling.
  4. Design the logistics. Decide vehicle, route, frequency, and labour. Batch collections to fill a truck rather than making half-load trips.
  5. Record everything. Keep a simple log: date, source, material, weight, cost, moisture. This data lets you calculate true cost per tonne and prove traceability to buyers.

Your target mix by volume should be roughly 2â3 parts carbon-rich material (stalks, straw, leaves, charcoal dust) to 1 part nitrogen-rich material (manure, vegetable waste, grass clippings), aiming for a C:N ratio of 25â30:1 and moisture of 50â60%. Test by squeezing a handful: it should feel like a wrung-out sponge.

5. Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Source list updated with contact name, phone, and agreed volume for every supplier.
  • â Carbon and nitrogen materials balanced at roughly 2â3:1 by volume before building the pile.
  • â All material chopped or shredded to 5â10 cm to speed decomposition.
  • â Manure and bone meal handled with gloves, boots, and (for bone meal) a respirator.
  • â No meat, dairy, plastic, glass, diseased plants, or herbicide-treated grass in the pile.
  • â Wood ash limited to 2â5% of pile volume; charcoal dust used for aeration, not nutrition.
  • â Every load weighed and logged with date, source, and cost.
  • â Collection route and vehicle schedule set; loads batched to avoid half-empty trips.
  • â Pile moisture checked weekly (target 50â60%) and turned on schedule.

6. Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â On-farm composting methods (Land and Water Discussion Paper 2)
  • FAO â Farmer field school guidance document on soil health and composting
  • Cornell University â Composting: Fundamentals and Applications (open access)
  • KALRO (Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation) â soil fertility and manure management bulletins
  • AGRA â Africa Agriculture Status Report and soil health training materials

quiz.q: What is the ideal size for chopping maize stalks for composting?
quiz.explanation: Smaller pieces decompose faster, and 5-10 cm is recommended.

quiz.q: Which crop residue is high in silica and decomposes slowly?
quiz.explanation: Rice straw contains high silica, making it slower to break down.

quiz.q: What ratio of crop residues to manure is suggested for good compost?
quiz.explanation: A 3:1 ratio of crop residues to manure balances carbon and nitrogen.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid composting diseased plants?
options: C) They can spread disease to healthy plants
quiz.explanation: Diseased plants can carry pathogens that survive composting and infect future crops.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: In dry areas, turning every two weeks helps maintain moisture and aeration.

quiz.q: Which animal manure has the highest nitrogen content?
quiz.explanation: Poultry manure contains about 3-5% nitrogen, the highest among common farm animals.

quiz.q: Which manure can be used fresh without burning plants?
quiz.explanation: Rabbit manure is mild and can be applied fresh without harming plants.

quiz.q: How much manure does a cow produce per day?
quiz.explanation: A cow produces about 10-15 kg of manure daily.

quiz.q: Why should you compost manure before using it on vegetables?
options: B) To kill pathogens and weed seeds
quiz.explanation: Composting at high temperatures kills harmful pathogens and weed seeds.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture level for a compost pile?
options: B) As moist as a wrung-out sponge
quiz.explanation: A wrung-out sponge moisture level supports microbial activity without waterlogging.

quiz.q: Which kitchen waste should you avoid in compost?
quiz.explanation: Meat and fish attract pests and create bad odors.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mix of kitchen waste to dry material?
quiz.explanation: A 1:2 ratio of kitchen waste to dry material controls moisture and odor.

quiz.q: Why should you limit citrus peels in compost?
options: B) They slow decomposition and repel worms
quiz.explanation: Citrus peels contain compounds that can inhibit decomposition and repel worms.

quiz.q: How much kitchen waste can a market stall generate daily?
quiz.explanation: A typical market stall can produce 5-10 kg of organic waste per day.

quiz.q: What should you do with kitchen waste to prevent flies?
options: B) Cover with dry material or soil
quiz.explanation: Covering fresh waste with dry material or soil reduces odors and flies.

quiz.q: Which weeds should you avoid composting?
quiz.explanation: Striga is an aggressive parasitic weed whose seeds survive composting.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid grass clippings from treated lawns?
options: B) They may contain herbicides that harm compost
quiz.explanation: Herbicides can persist and damage plants when the compost is used.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ratio of dry leaves to fresh grass clippings?
quiz.explanation: A 2:1 ratio of dry leaves to grass clippings balances carbon and nitrogen.

quiz.q: Which leaves decompose slowly and should be used in small amounts?
quiz.explanation: Oak leaves are acidic and slow to break down.

quiz.q: How much dry leaves can a large tree provide per season?
quiz.explanation: A large tree can yield 50-100 kg of dry leaves per season.

quiz.q: What nutrient is wood ash high in?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash contains 5-10% potassium, along with calcium and trace minerals.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid ash from charcoal briquettes?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal briquettes often contain additives that can harm soil.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of wood ash to add to compost?
quiz.explanation: A small amount, about 1 cup per 10 kg, is enough to add minerals without over-alkalizing.

quiz.q: What does charcoal dust add to compost?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal dust is pure carbon and improves soil structure and nutrient retention.

quiz.q: How is bone meal made?
options: B) By boiling, drying, and crushing bones
C) By soaking bones in water
quiz.explanation: Bone meal is made by boiling bones to remove meat, drying, and crushing them.

quiz.q: What nutrient is bone meal high in?
quiz.explanation: Bone meal contains 15-20% phosphorus, essential for root development.

quiz.q: How much raw material is needed to produce 1 ton of compost per month?
quiz.explanation: About 3 tons of raw materials are needed to produce 1 ton of finished compost.

quiz.q: What is a good way to secure steady supply of materials?
options: B) Make agreements with restaurants and markets
D) Use only your own waste
quiz.explanation: Agreements with regular waste producers ensure a consistent supply.

quiz.q: What is the recommended layering for a compost pile?
quiz.explanation: Layering 15 cm dry and 10 cm wet materials balances carbon and nitrogen.

quiz.q: Why is it important to track collection costs?
quiz.explanation: Knowing costs helps set a price that covers expenses and yields profit.
